title: How many ways can we write twelve?
description: The number twelve is written as an adding, a taking away, a multiplying and a dividing sentence, each with two numbers. All four work out to the same value. Keeko doubts that different looking sentences can share one value.
teaching_notes: One idea: expressions that look different can have the same value, so equal means the same value on both sides. Watch for children who think different expressions must give different values.

source: Write four different expressions whose value is 12, and one more for a favourite number of your own.
video_script.why: The child sees that one value can be reached by all four operations.
video_script.substitution: Use the four operations in turn to reach the same number, twelve.
video_script.anchor: Four expressions that all have the value twelve
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko believes expressions that look different must work out to different numbers, so ten plus two and fifteen minus three cannot both be twelve.
video_script.payoff_line: All four expressions have the value twelve

final_answer.spoken: ten plus two, fifteen minus three, three times four and twenty four divided by two all have the value twelve

never_show: an expression whose value is not 12
maths_rules: different looking expressions can have the same value
video_script.design: One idea: one value, many expressions. Assumes the four operations. Wrong idea: different expressions must have different values. The number twelve stays at the centre of the board all video.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the number 12 in a ring at the centre of the board

marks.book: the title card arrives: From your book
marks.ask: the ring around 12 glows and four empty boxes appear around it

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the number twelve.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many different ways can we write twelve, using two numbers and one operation?

beats.on_screen: the ring and the four empty boxes stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: four boxes labelled adding, taking away, multiplying, dividing around the ring 12

marks.ops: the four operation boxes light up one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='ops'/>An expression joins two numbers with one of four operations: adding, taking away, multiplying or dividing.
<bookmark mark='target'/>The number each expression works out to must be twelve.

beats.on_screen: Given: the number 12; two numbers; the four operations + − × ÷

marks.given: the number and the four signs are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the number twelve, two numbers to use, and the four operations.

beats.on_screen: To find: four different expressions with value 12

marks.find: the words four different expressions are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write four different expressions whose value is twelve.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Step one, use adding. Ten and two join to make twelve, because ten plus two is twelve.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Step two, use taking away. If we take three from fifteen, twelve is left.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Step three, use multiplying. Three lots of four make twelve, so three times four is twelve.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Step four, use dividing. Twenty four shared into two equal parts gives twelve, so twenty four divided by two is twelve.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 10 + 2, 15 − 3, 3 × 4 and 24 ÷ 2 all have the value 12; the same four ways work for a favourite number such as 20

marks.ans: the four boxes are joined to 12 and boxed
marks.own: the favourite number 20 appears with its own four boxes

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>All four expressions have the value twelve.
<bookmark mark='own'/>Any favourite number, such as twenty, can be written in the same four ways.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows: different looking expressions give different values; 10 + 2 and 15 − 3 side by side both reach 12; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.fix: 10 + 2 and 15 − 3 both reach 12 and the bubble is struck through

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks expressions that look different must have different values.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But ten plus two and fifteen minus three look different, and both work out to twelve. Looking different does not change the value.
